name: Jaguar Kings and Feathered Serpents: Ancient Mexico
description: Three thousand years of Mesoamerica, from the first maize farmers and the Olmec heads to Maya cities, the Aztec capital and the Spanish conquest that ended it.

checkpoints.name: Maize and the Olmecs
checkpoints.note: Farmers turn a wild grass into maize, and cacao comes north to be drunk as a bitter, frothy drink. People play the Mesoamerican ballgame with rubber balls. On the Gulf coast the Olmecs carve colossal stone heads and lay out some of the earliest great ceremonial centres.

checkpoints.name: The Classic cities
checkpoints.note: The Zapotecs rule Oaxaca from a levelled mountaintop. The Maya civilization raises Tikal and Palenque, writes in the Maya script and counts time with the Maya calendar, while Teotihuacan grows into a vast city of pyramids. At Palenque, Pakal the Great reigns for nearly seventy years.

checkpoints.name: Collapse and renewal
checkpoints.note: In the Classic Maya collapse, drought, war and political breakdown empty many southern cities, though Maya people stay. In the north Chichen Itza flourishes, the Toltecs rule from Tula, and farmers in the Valley of Mexico build chinampas, fields raised out of the lake.

checkpoints.name: The Aztec world
checkpoints.note: The Mexica found Tenochtitlan on an island in a lake and raise the Templo Mayor to their gods. From 1428 the Aztec Empire takes tribute from much of central Mexico, and Aztec religion demands human sacrifice. The voyages of Columbus reach the Caribbean from 1492, and Moctezuma II takes the throne in 1502.

checkpoints.name: Conquest
checkpoints.note: Hernan Cortes lands in 1519 and wins Indigenous allies, with La Malinche as his interpreter. Moctezuma II dies in Spanish custody in 1520. Smallpox sweeps the city, and in 1521 Cuauhtemoc, the last emperor, is captured as the Spanish Conquest of the Aztec Empire ends.

checkpoints.name: New Spain
checkpoints.note: New Spain is ruled from Mexico City, built on the ruins of Tenochtitlan. Friars write Nahuatl in Latin letters, Maya writers record the Popol Vuh, and the Florentine Codex preserves Aztec life in words and pictures. The Columbian Exchange reshapes farms, and the last Maya kingdom falls in 1697.
